DOCUMENT:
Incident Report: Partial Racking Collapse, Aisle 14
Daventry Distribution Centre, Health, Safety and Operations, 18 September 2026

1. Summary of the incident
At 02:47 on 3 September 2026, a reach truck reversing out of aisle 14 struck the front upright of bay 14-22. The upright buckled, and two adjacent bays of pallet racking (14-22 and 14-23) partially collapsed, bringing down 46 pallets of ambient grocery stock from levels 2 to 5. The aisle was unoccupied apart from the driver, who was uninjured. The area was cordoned off within ten minutes and the night shift manager stopped all work in aisles 13 to 15.

2. Immediate response
A racking inspector attended at 07:30 and confirmed that the damage was confined to the two bays. Damaged stock was removed under supervision over the following two days, and the replacement uprights and beams were fitted on 9 September. The aisle reopened on 10 September after a full inspection.

3. Losses
Of the 46 pallets brought down, 18 were written off entirely, at an average stock value of £2,400 per pallet, a loss of £43,200. The remaining 28 pallets were partially damaged, with an average loss after re-sorting of £650 per pallet, a further £21,800. Racking repair and inspection cost £14,800. Total direct cost of the incident was therefore £79,800, excluding lost productivity in aisles 13 to 15 for the six days the area was restricted.

4. Investigation
The driver, employed through our labour agency, had worked at the site for five weeks and held a valid reach-truck licence. CCTV shows the truck reversing at an angle and at a speed the investigating manager judged to be within site limits, before the rear of the truck contacted the upright. The driver stated he was looking over his shoulder at the time but that the upright was obscured by a pallet overhanging the adjacent bay.

The site racking inspection log shows that the upright at 14-22 had been recorded as amber damage (a dent requiring repair within four weeks, with the bay offloaded if not repaired) during the inspection of 2 July, nine weeks before the collapse. No repair or offloading had been carried out. The log also shows 14 other amber items across the site that are past their four-week repair deadline.

5. Protection measures
In 2025 we fitted steel rack-end and upright protectors to aisles 1 to 8. Since then, aisles 1 to 8 have logged 3 reported racking strikes, compared with 19 in aisles 9 to 16. Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes, and fitting them to aisles 9 to 16 would be expected to reduce strikes there by a similar proportion. Aisles 1 to 8 hold slow-moving reserve stock and account for about a fifth of reach-truck movements on site.

6. Root cause
The investigation concludes that the root cause was driver error: an inexperienced agency driver reversing without a clear line of sight. Contributing factors were the overhanging pallet in bay 14-21 and the absence of upright protectors in aisle 14.

7. Actions
7.1 All agency reach-truck drivers to complete an additional site-specific practical assessment, including reversing in aisles, before working unsupervised. Owner: Training Manager. Due: 30 October.
7.2 Fit upright protectors to aisles 9 to 16, at an estimated cost of £22,000. Owner: Facilities Manager. Due: 30 November.
7.3 Reinforce the pallet overhang check in the put-away procedure and include it in team briefings. Owner: Night Shift Manager. Due: immediately.
7.4 Share this report with the labour agency and request a review of how drivers are assessed before placement.

8. Conclusion
This was a serious incident that could have caused injury. With retraining of agency drivers and protectors in the remaining aisles, we are satisfied that the risk of recurrence has been addressed and that normal operations can continue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "with an average loss after re-sorting of £650 per pallet, a further £21,800" -- 28 pallets x £650 = £18,200, not £21,800. The total direct cost should therefore be £43,200 + £18,200 + £14,800 = £76,200, not £79,800.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes, and fitting them to aisles 9 to 16 would be expected to reduce strikes there by a similar proportion." -- The comparison is confounded: the document notes aisles 1 to 8 hold slow-moving stock and see only about a fifth of reach-truck movements, so far fewer strikes would be expected there regardless. Protectors also mitigate damage from strikes rather than prevent them. The data do not show protectors cause fewer strikes.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "The investigation concludes that the root cause was driver error" -- The report's own evidence shows the upright had been logged as amber damage nine weeks earlier and was neither repaired nor offloaded, and that 14 other amber items are overdue. The failed inspection-repair process is a direct contributing cause and live site-wide risk, yet the root cause, actions and conclusion that recurrence risk 'has been addressed' never address it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Incident Report, Partial Racking Collapse, Aisle 14

The incident narrative is clear and well sequenced. However, the report's own evidence points to a different root cause than the one it names. The cost figure contains an arithmetic error. The protector evidence doesn't show what the cover note says it shows. Together, these mean the conclusion that "normal operations can safely continue" isn't supported yet.

## 1. The root cause section leaves out the most important finding

Section 4 says the upright at 14-22 was **recorded as amber damage on 2 July**. Under your own standard, it should have been repaired by about 30 July or the bay offloaded. Neither happened, and the bay stayed fully loaded on levels 2 to 5 for nine weeks. A previously damaged upright that buckles on a reversing strike, at a speed judged within site limits, is a strong sign that the failure was in **damage management, not only driving**.

Section 6 doesn't mention this at all, and no action addresses it. As written, the report blames an agency driver with a valid licence who was driving within limits. Meanwhile, a known, logged defect that should have been fixed or offloaded goes unexamined. Readers such as an HSE inspector, insurer or auditor will likely notice this first.

**Suggested fixes:**
- Revise section 6 so the overdue amber repair is a primary cause, or at least a co-equal one. Consider whether "driver error" is the right framing for a licensed driver within speed limits whose view was blocked by a put-away failure.
- Investigate why the amber item wasn't actioned. Who receives the inspection log? Who authorises repairs and offloading? Was there a budget or contractor backlog? The cover note mentions interviews with the driver and shift manager only. Nobody responsible for the inspection regime appears to have been spoken to.
- Add an action with an owner and date to close out amber items within deadline, with escalation and mandatory offloading when deadlines are missed.

## 2. Fourteen overdue amber items mean the risk is still live

The log shows **14 other amber items past their repair deadline**. These are the same condition that preceded this collapse. Until they are repaired or the bays offloaded, the statement in section 8 that "the risk of recurrence has been addressed" is not accurate. This is the most urgent practical point in the review.

**Suggested fix:** Add an immediate action to inspect all 14 items, then offload or repair each one, with a completion date. Make the "operations can continue" conclusion depend on that being done.

## 3. The cost figure is wrong

28 pallets × £650 = **£18,200**, not £21,800. The corrected total is:

| Item | Stated | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Written off (18 × £2,400) | £43,200 | £43,200 |
| Partially damaged (28 × £650) | £21,800 | **£18,200** |
| Racking repair and inspection | £14,800 | £14,800 |
| **Total** | **£79,800** | **£76,200** |

The total adds up correctly from the wrong line, which suggests a transposition (18,200 → 21,800). Either the £650 average or the £21,800 figure is wrong. Check against the stock reconciliation before calling the figure "firm."

## 4. The protector evidence is weaker than presented

The cover note calls this "before-and-after evidence." It isn't. Section 5 compares **different aisles over the same period**. It doesn't compare the same aisles before and after fitting. The comparison also has several problems:

- **Unequal traffic.** Aisles 1 to 8 handle about a fifth of reach-truck movements and hold slow-moving reserve stock. Adjusted for traffic (roughly 20% vs 80% of movements), the strike rate is about 3/20 vs 19/80, or **0.15 vs 0.24 per unit of traffic**. That is roughly a one-third reduction, not the six-fold difference that 3 vs 19 implies. Slow-moving reserve aisles also have less congestion and fewer put-aways, so even that difference may not be due to protectors.
- **What is being counted.** Protectors don't stop trucks hitting racking. They absorb the impact. A strike on a protector may not be logged as a "racking strike," so lower counts may partly reflect how strikes are recorded. The claim "Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes" should be reworded.
- **No time period** is given for the comparison.

Protectors are still very likely a sensible, proportionate measure for high-traffic aisles. The recommendation stands. The justification should be stated honestly.

**Suggested rewording:** "Protectors reduce the consequence of strikes on uprights. Aisles 1 to 8 have recorded fewer strikes than aisles 9 to 16 since fitting, though these aisles carry far less traffic and the figures are not directly comparable. We recommend fitting protectors to aisles 9 to 16 given their higher traffic and the consequences seen in this incident." Better still, compare strike counts in aisles 1 to 8 before and after 2025, if the data exists.

## 5. Actions don't fully match the cover note's description

- **7.4 has no owner and no due date.** The cover note says all actions have named owners and dates.
- **7.3** ("immediately," "reinforce," "include in briefings") is hard to verify. Consider adding a measurable check, such as overhang checks recorded in put-away audits for a set period.
- **7.1** applies only to agency drivers. If reversing with blocked sightlines is the hazard, it isn't specific to agency staff. Consider applying the assessment to all reach-truck drivers, or explain why it doesn't need to.
- **No action addresses the inspection and repair regime** (see sections 1 and 2 above).
- **Line of sight:** consider whether aisle layout, mirrors, cameras or reversing aids are worth assessing, rather than relying only on driver behaviour.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Conclusion timing.** The report is dated 18 September, but protectors aren't due until 30 November and the assessment until 30 October. "Has been addressed" should read "will be addressed once these actions are complete." Today is 13 November, so it's worth confirming whether 7.1 was completed on time.
- **Independent inspection.** The cover note says the racking was "independently inspected." Section 2 only says "a racking inspector attended." If they were external or SEMA-approved, say so, because it strengthens the report.
- **Overhanging pallet.** The report notes it but doesn't say how it got there or how long it had been there. Was it a one-off put-away error or a recurring issue? This affects whether 7.3 goes far enough.
- **Restriction period.** "Six days" (3 to 10 September) is reasonable, but say whether it counts calendar days or shifts.

## Summary of recommended changes

1. Reframe the root cause to include the unactioned amber damage, and investigate why it was missed.
2. Add an urgent action covering the 14 overdue amber items, and make the "operations can continue" conclusion depend on it.
3. Correct the partial-damage line to £18,200 and the total to £76,200 (after checking the source data).
4. Reword section 5 to drop "clearly prevent" and to acknowledge the traffic difference. Remove "before-and-after" from the cover note.
5. Give 7.4 an owner and date, make 7.3 measurable, and consider widening 7.1.
6. Soften the conclusion so it reflects actions still in progress.

With these changes, the report would be accurate and defensible, and much more useful in preventing a repeat.
